earth-formation.summary: Accretion of the Earth from the solar nebula, dated by radiometric analysis of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial minerals.
earth-formation.significance: Everything else on this timeline is compressed into the last tenth of it. If the Earth's history were a single day, recorded human history would occupy the final second.

origin-of-life.summary: Self-replicating chemistry appeared within a few hundred million years of the Earth becoming habitable — startlingly fast, which is one reason the question of life elsewhere stays open.
origin-of-life.significance: Life appeared almost as soon as the planet could support it. That speed is the main reason biologists take the possibility of life elsewhere seriously.
origin-of-life.note: Carbon isotope signatures in Greenland zircons hint at 4.1 Ga; undisputed microfossils are closer to 3.5 Ga. How life began remains unsolved.

great-oxidation.summary: Cyanobacteria filled the atmosphere with oxygen, poisoning most existing life and rusting the oceans. The largest pollution event in history, and the reason anything breathes today.
great-oxidation.significance: The first mass extinction was caused by a lifeform poisoning its own atmosphere. It is also the reason anything can breathe.

eukaryotes.summary: One cell engulfed another and kept it, producing the mitochondrion. Every plant, animal and fungus descends from that single merger.

image.credit: Daniel Vaulot, CNRS, Station Biologique de Roscoff

multicellular-life.summary: Cells began staying together and specialising, producing the soft frond-like Ediacaran organisms that preceded the Cambrian and mostly left no descendants.
